title: ₹100 Crore and Counting: 'Raja Shivaji' Just Shattered Every Record in Marathi Cinema
excerpt: Riteish Deshmukh's historical epic is on the verge of becoming the first Marathi film ever to cross the ₹100 crore mark — and it's not slowing down.
body:
For decades, Marathi cinema has lived in Bollywood's shadow at the box office. Critically celebrated, culturally vital, but commercially modest — the industry's biggest hits rarely crossed the ₹50 crore mark. 'Sairat' broke through with ₹110 crore in 2016, but that felt like lightning in a bottle.

Now, Riteish Deshmukh's 'Raja Shivaji' is rewriting the script entirely — and doing it with a historical epic that Marathi audiences and Hindi-speaking viewers are embracing with equal fervour.

The Numbers Tell the Story

As of Day 16, 'Raja Shivaji' has grossed approximately ₹96 crore in India, with ₹81 crore in net collections. The Marathi version has contributed around ₹56 crore, while the simultaneous Hindi release has added ₹23 crore — a dual-language strategy that has dramatically expanded the film's reach beyond Maharashtra.

The film has already surpassed 'Baipan Bhari Deva' (₹90.50 crore) to become the second-highest-grossing Marathi film ever. 'Sairat's all-time record of ₹110 crore is now firmly in range, with trade analysts projecting a lifetime collection of ₹125 crore or more.

What Makes It Work

'Raja Shivaji' is not a small film pretending to be big. Riteish Deshmukh — who directed and stars — assembled a cast that bridges Marathi and Hindi cinema: Sanjay Dutt and Vidya Balan bring Bollywood draw, while the story's roots are deeply Marathi. The music by Ajay-Atul, arguably India's hottest film composers after their 'RRR' and 'Pushpa' work, provides an emotional backbone that works across languages.

The subject matter is inherently powerful. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj is not just a historical figure in Maharashtra — he's a cultural icon whose story resonates with pride, resistance, and identity. The film taps into that emotional current without veering into propaganda, delivering a historical action drama that respects its audience's intelligence.

The Dual-Language Gamble

The most fascinating aspect of 'Raja Shivaji's success is its dual-language release. Previous Marathi hits have been dubbed into Hindi after theatrical runs, but releasing simultaneously in both languages was a calculated risk. It could have diluted the Marathi audience by cannibalising showcount, or the Hindi version could have flopped without an audience that connected to the story.

Neither happened. The Hindi version found audiences in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Delhi-NCR, and even South India — viewers who responded to the historical epic regardless of linguistic origin. This is the 'Baahubali' effect in miniature: a great story, well told, transcends regional boundaries.

Why Maharashtrian NRIs Are Celebrating

For the Maharashtrian diaspora — concentrated in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia — 'Raja Shivaji's success feels deeply personal. International screenings in cities with significant Marathi populations — Pune expats in the Bay Area, Mumbaikars in London's Wembley, families in Toronto's Mississauga — have reported strong turnout.

The film's success is validating a long-held belief in the diaspora: that Marathi stories deserve the same scale and ambition as Hindi or Telugu productions. When NRI families book weekend showings of 'Raja Shivaji' at AMC or Cineplex, they're not just watching a movie — they're affirming that their language and culture can command a blockbuster screen.

What's Next for Marathi Cinema

'Raja Shivaji' crossing ₹100 crore isn't just a number — it's a threshold. It proves to producers and distributors that Marathi films can justify large budgets, multi-language releases, and Bollywood-tier marketing spends. The question now is whether the industry can sustain this momentum, or whether 'Raja Shivaji' becomes another one-off like 'Sairat.'

Riteish Deshmukh, who has long straddled both industries, may have just built the bridge that Marathi cinema needed. The ₹100 crore club now has a new member — and it speaks Marathi.
